brief.researchQuestion: On the apprenticeship account, a junior who mostly clears exception lists should learn judgement about evidence more slowly, yet I half-remember a couple of juniors on an automated client who seemed to learn faster. I'm unsure whether that pattern is real, and a real pattern would be a puzzle for both the apprenticeship account and Beane's shadow learning, because those juniors were learning inside the approved route.
brief.context: I'd study audit engagement teams at one of the large accounting firms, maybe the firm where I used to work, on engagements where the firm has adopted automated testing tools, although I still need to arrange access. The unit is the junior auditor, and the engagement team (a partner, a manager, one or two seniors and a few juniors working at the client's office under deadline pressure) is the setting where juniors learn, though I'm keeping open whether the engagement team is the unit. I'm drawn to this setting because I know audit work and because the shift to automated testing is happening now, so juniors who start this year will do much less testing by hand than I did. Outside the engagement team, the regulator uses its inspections to push firms to document every judgement, seniors respond to that pressure in the points that they ask juniors to record, and the firm decides through its methodology which tests the tool runs. I'm less sure about the client's part.
brief.siteRationale: My former firm is the obvious site, because I know people there and because the firm was already automating when I left, so the firm should have both heavily and lightly automated engagements, and a single firm keeps the methodology and tools constant while the amount of automation varies by client. The firm is also the right place because juniors exercise judgement there, both in the file and in their exchanges with the senior. Access is my main worry, because my contacts are all juniors or seniors, because a partner or the risk and quality team would choose the engagements, and because whoever made that choice might steer me towards the better-run engagements, in which case I may see too few of the juniors who struggle. I'll also see little of the learning that juniors do away from the engagement. As far as I remember, the firm used the analytics mostly on big clients with clean data, so heavily automated engagements may have bigger, better-staffed teams, and I'd be comparing kinds of client as much as levels of automation.
brief.processOfInterest: I'd look at a junior's first busy season, roughly October to March, because the audit team does most of its testing in those months. The phenomenon is each junior's judgement about whether audit evidence is enough, and I'd follow that judgement on engagements where juniors do the routine testing and on engagements where juniors clear the exceptions that the tool flags, although I'm still unsure whether "enough" is the right word. If juniors learn by doing the routine work, a junior who only receives exception lists should progress more slowly, yet I half-remember a couple of juniors on an automated client who seemed to progress faster, and I'm uncertain whether that impression is real. My best candidate for tracking the change in that judgement is the exception log, in which the junior records a disposition and a short explanation for each item that the tool flags, together with the senior's review notes on that log. If a junior writes fuller explanations over the season, or the senior writes fewer review notes, I might read that pattern as a sign of learning, although I'm unsure whether juniors write enough in the log for me to tell.
brief.outcomeOfInterest: The outcome is the quality of a junior's judgement about evidence by the end of the first busy season. I'd expect some juniors to finish that season able to spot insufficient evidence while others are still just following the programme, and my question is whether the gap between those two groups is wider or narrower on heavily automated engagements than on lightly automated engagements, which means comparing juniors on the two kinds of engagement at the end of the same season. If the apprenticeship view is right, the juniors on heavily automated engagements should finish the season weaker, although I'm unsure whether that prediction is right. To place each junior, I'd combine the junior's written explanations in the file with an interview about a borderline item, and perhaps the seniors' view. The answer matters because firms are deciding now how to train juniors, and if the old apprenticeship has lapsed, the part that the apprenticeship played in training juniors may now be vacant.
brief.bind: I think the tension is between speed and learning. The firm wants to clear the exceptions within budget and also wants juniors to develop judgement, although learning needs more time than the firm has budgeted. Seniors feel the tension in deciding whether to stop and ask or to fix the wording themselves, and juniors feel the tension in deciding whether to look into an odd item or to write a safe, standard explanation and so look quick. I'd guess that partners feel the tension less, because they see the budget more than the learning. I'm working from my own time as a junior, and the seniors whom I remember stopping to ask had themselves been juniors on that client, so the teaching may depend on the senior as much as on the tool.
brief.sampleRationale: My main comparison is between juniors on heavily automated engagements and juniors on lightly automated engagements over the same busy season, and I'd also like to compare first-years with third-years, since the third-years did most of their first season by hand before the firm introduced the tools. I'd want to keep the firm and the service line constant, and ideally client size as well, though I'm unsure whether I can keep client size constant, because the heavily automated engagements may turn out to be mostly with the big clients. I think I'd need maybe three heavily automated and three lightly automated engagements, ideally in pairs of similar size, although I doubt that I could match the pairs well; on each engagement I'd follow the first-year juniors and interview a third-year and the senior, with eight to twelve juniors altogether (I'm guessing at those numbers), including some juniors who struggle. I think the senior matters more than client size, because if the heavily automated engagements also have the more experienced seniors, who ask juniors to explain, I'd end up crediting the tool with the seniors' effect, and since I have to take the seniors as I find them, I'd be describing the overlap more than removing it. The whole design depends on the firm's permission, and I have yet to gain access.
brief.earlySurprise: My evidence is very thin, since it consists of two informal pilot conversations with former colleagues, which I wrote up from memory. The surprise is that both stories fit within one firm, because some juniors might learn a lot from the exception list and others very little, depending on whether each junior copies or chases, and I'd want to explore the reasons that lead a junior to chase. I also noticed that in both stories someone above the junior shaped the explanations: Colleague A rewrites the explanations herself near the deadline, and on Colleague B's automated engagement the manager had written a standard set of explanations. So whether a junior copies or chases might depend on the senior's or manager's handling of the exception list, and I'd next want to examine that handling alongside the juniors themselves. I'd also want to find out whether the first-years' explanations were wrong or just slow when Colleague A rewrote them, and whether the juniors ever saw Colleague A's version, because the juniors can learn from Colleague A's version only if they see that version.
brief.startingInterest: I'm interested in AI and early-career professional work, and in audit in particular, where I worked as a junior for two years before the PhD. Juniors in audit learn judgement by doing routine testing, such as sampling, vouching and reconciliations, under a senior's review, and I now think that juniors learned much of that judgement from the seniors' review notes and the seniors' questions. Because audit firms are automating the routine testing, I want to find the place in which juniors will learn judgement now, and to see whether the review of flagged exceptions might become that place. I'm still unsure whether my assumption about the way that juniors used to learn judgement is right.

brief.puzzleAnswer: On the apprenticeship account, a firm that takes routine tasks away from juniors starves those juniors of practice, and so juniors on heavily automated engagements should learn judgement more slowly. I half-remember a different pattern, though: a couple of juniors on a big automated client seemed to learn faster, maybe because they spent their days on the exceptions that the tool flagged. I'm unsure whether the pattern was real or whether I'm being kind in my memory of two bright people. If the pattern is real, it falls outside both the apprenticeship account and Beane's shadow learning, because those juniors were learning inside the approved route, on the work that the firm gave them. In the exception log I'd then expect the junior to give the reason that an item looked odd and to give a view on whether the item was fine, and I'd expect the senior to ask fewer questions about the same kind of item over the season. By contrast, if I found short, repeated explanations and bare sign-offs, I'd take those entries as a sign that the pattern is illusory. I'm also wary that many of the flagged items may be false positives that juniors clear by habit, in which case the exception work could starve those juniors in a different way.

Pilot conversation 1 was informal and took place outside any interview format, and I wrote up the conversation from memory the same evening.

Colleague A worked as a junior with me at my old firm and is now a senior. We met for coffee, and I asked Colleague A about her current engagement, a large listed retailer where the firm runs its analytics tool over the whole ledger.

Colleague A said that her first-years spend most of their time on the exception list. Of roughly four hundred flagged items in the revenue test, she thought that most were false positives, such as credit notes with the wrong posting date. According to Colleague A, the juniors clear those false positives quickly and "learn the client's quirks" from them.

Colleague A mentioned one first-year who kept returning to her with questions about the same supplier's credit notes until he established that the client had changed its returns policy. She said that he "learned more from that than I did from a whole year of vouching". She also said that most of the first-years just copy last year's explanations from the prior-year file.

Colleague A said that she rewrites a lot of the explanations herself near the deadline, because rewriting them is quicker.

My notes: this account is one person's view of one engagement, and because Colleague A is a friend, she may have told me the story that she thought I wanted to hear.

Pilot conversation 2 was an informal chat, outside the interview format, and I wrote up these notes from memory the next morning.

Colleague B was a junior with me at my old firm and is now a third-year, and we spoke on the phone. Colleague B's main engagement is a mid-sized manufacturing group, where the team still selects and vouches samples by hand because the client keeps its data across several systems.

He said that his first-years "tick and bash" through samples for most of the busy season, and that he can tell within a month which first-years will be good, because the good ones ask him about a number that moved before he asks them. He also said that the review notes are mostly about missing references and presentation.

On his previous engagement, where the audit team used the analytics tool, he said the juniors were "faster but shallower", and he worried that they'd gone through the work without looking at a single actual invoice. When I asked about the exception list, he said that the juniors cleared the list with a standard set of explanations that the manager had written.

My notes: I read Colleague B's account as cutting against Colleague A's story, although Colleague B was comparing two different clients and also said he'd spent only three weeks on the automated engagement.

I only have two informal pilot conversations with former colleagues, which I wrote up from memory, so this evidence is very thin. The first colleague, a senior on a heavily automated retail client, told me about a first-year who learned a lot by chasing the same supplier's credit notes until he found that the client had changed its returns policy, although the senior also said that most first-years just copy last year's explanations. The second colleague, a third-year on a manual client, said that the juniors on the automated engagement that he'd seen were "faster but shallower" and cleared exceptions with the manager's standard explanations.

The surprise for me is that both stories fit within one firm, because some juniors might learn a lot from the exception list and other juniors very little, depending on whether each junior copies or chases. I'd want to explore the reasons that lead a junior to chase.
